title: API 653 Training in Salt Lake City: Tank Inspector Exam Prep
description: Self-paced API 653 exam prep for Salt Lake City tank inspectors: refinery tank farms, heated waxy crude, pipeline terminals, acid storage and seismic risk.
h1: API 653 Training in Salt Lake City: Aboveground Storage Tank Inspector Exam Prep for Refinery Tank Farms, Terminals and Industrial Storage
html:
API 653 exam prep for tank inspectors in the Salt Lake area

Storage tanks around Salt Lake City fall into three groups. The largest is the tankage inside and beside the valley's five refineries, which hold crude, intermediates and finished products. The second is pipeline and terminal storage on the systems that carry crude into the valley and products out of it. The third is industrial storage that has nothing to do with fuel, most visibly the sulfuric acid made at the copper smelter on the west side of the valley. All three employ API 653 inspectors, either directly or through the contractors that serve them.

This page is for tank inspectors, terminal staff, NDT technicians and engineers who want to sit API 653 from Salt Lake City. It sets out where the tanks are and which rules bring an inspector to them, explains what heated waxy crude, concentrated acid, earthquakes and snow mean for a tank programme here, and works through one roof assessment. There is no Atlantis classroom in Salt Lake City; you prepare online at your own pace, and an instructor answers your questions.

Refinery tank farms and the terminal beside Marathon's plant

EIA's 2026 refinery capacity survey lists five operating refineries in Utah with a combined crude distillation capacity of 213,089 barrels per calendar day: Marathon Petroleum's and Chevron's plants in Salt Lake City, Big West Oil's in North Salt Lake, and HF Sinclair's and Silver Eagle Refining's in Woods Cross. Each runs its own tank farm, and between them they store crude received by pipeline and by truck as well as the gasoline, distillates and other products they ship.

The truck traffic is distinctive. Marathon describes the waxy crude unloading facility at the terminal next to its Salt Lake City refinery, rebuilt with five unloading lanes in place of two, which handles roughly 100 transport trucks a day and moves the crude by pipe into refinery tankage. That crude comes from the Uinta Basin, and Utah's Department of Environmental Quality notes that it has to be heated in the field and hauled in insulated trucks because it solidifies quickly. Tanks that receive it are a different inspection job from a gasoline tank, as the section on heated tanks below explains.

Pipeline tanks north, south and east of the valley

Salt Lake tank inspectors also travel. Three pipeline systems tie the valley to its supply and its markets, and each has storage along it:

  • Crude from Wyoming. The Frontier Aspen pipeline brings Canadian and Rocky Mountain crudes 289 miles from Casper to Frontier Station in Utah, and the SLC pipeline carries crude on into the Salt Lake area. Both sit within Holly Energy Partners, now part of HF Sinclair.
  • Products south. The UNEV pipeline, owned by an HF Sinclair subsidiary, runs from Woods Cross to the Las Vegas valley. Its Cedar City terminal occupies a 30-acre site, and its North Las Vegas terminal at Apex has 330,000 barrels of storage.
  • Products north. The Salt Lake products system, now under tariffs of Tesoro Logistics Northwest Pipeline LLC published by MPLX, runs from Salt Lake Station in Davis County to Burley, Pocatello and Boise in Idaho and Pasco in Washington. When Tesoro agreed to buy the system from Chevron, its terminals at Boise, Pocatello and Pasco held 1.3 million barrels of storage between them.

Where a tank on one of those systems is a pipeline breakout tank, federal rules decide its inspection. Under 49 CFR 195.432, atmospheric and low-pressure steel breakout tanks must be inspected according to API Standard 653, except its section 6.4.3, so the risk-based internal inspection interval cannot be used to set the internal interval. PHMSA proposed in June 2026 to allow risk-based intervals for breakout tanks, with caps for the first and later internal inspections, and to update the referenced API 653 from the third to the fifth edition. At the time of writing that was a proposal, so check the current text of the rule before relying on it.

Why Utah's tank programme stops at the refinery fence

Utah's Division of Environmental Response and Remediation began regulating certain aboveground petroleum storage tanks in 2021. The programme covers petroleum tanks larger than 500 gallons that rest on soil or gravel, or that have piping below ground, and it requires registration, financial responsibility and a certificate of compliance supported by tank and line tightness tests. It also excludes several categories outright, including petroleum refiners, petroleum bulk stations and terminals, and tanks related to oil and gas production and gathering.

So the state programme does not reach the refinery and terminal tanks that employ most API 653 inspectors in the valley. Their inspection is driven by three other things:

  1. The federal SPCC rule. Under 40 CFR 112.8(c)(6), onshore facilities must test or inspect each aboveground bulk storage container for integrity on a regular schedule and whenever material repairs are made. EPA's guidance leaves the owner to choose the industry standard and names API 653 and STI SP001 as two commonly used inspection standards for aboveground bulk storage.
  2. Pipeline rules, for breakout tanks, as above.
  3. The owner's own programme, which at a refinery commonly adopts API 653 for its API 650 tanks whatever the regulator requires.

Heated tanks for waxy crude

Keeping waxy crude liquid changes several things an API 653 inspector looks at. Heated tanks are usually insulated, so the shell and roof can corrode under the insulation where water gets past damaged cladding or seals, and the inspector has to decide how much insulation to remove to judge the steel beneath. Internal heating coils bring their own leaks, supports and condensate, and a coil that fails can put water into the product. Wax and sludge settle on the floor, which lengthens cleaning before an internal inspection and can hide pitting until the floor is properly cleaned and scanned.

Temperature also matters for design. API 650 has an annex for tanks designed for elevated temperatures, which applies above 200°F and changes the allowable stress basis. The current API 653 Body of Knowledge leaves that annex out apart from its scope clause but keeps required thickness for elevated temperatures among the calculations, so concentrate on how API 653 evaluates a heated tank in service and on the damage mechanisms in API RP 571 that heat accelerates, corrosion under insulation among them.

Sulfuric acid storage at the copper smelter

Rio Tinto Kennecott describes itself as one of America's largest producers of sulfuric acid, made as a by-product of copper smelting and sold at a concentration of 93 to 98 percent. It ships acid in its own fleet of rail tank cars, about 100 tons a car, and by truck in loads of 25 to 35 tons. Storage and loading of that much acid is tank work, and owners of carbon steel acid tanks can apply API 653 methods to them.

Concentrated sulfuric acid is usually stored in carbon steel because the steel forms a protective sulfate film. That film is what an inspector is really assessing: dilution with moisture, high velocity at inlet nozzles and warm product all break it down, so the vapour space, the roof, the shell near inlets and the area where acid splashes deserve close attention. API RP 571 describes sulfuric acid corrosion and is the reference to study. Exam questions on chemical service tend to test the principle that the fluid, its concentration and its temperature drive the damage, not the tank's construction code.

Earthquakes, snow and cold on the Wasatch Front

A US Geological Survey fact sheet from 2016 puts the probability of at least one magnitude 6.75 or larger earthquake in the Wasatch Front region within 50 years at 43 percent, and of magnitude 6.0 or larger at 57 percent. For a tank owner that means anchorage, the shell-to-bottom junction, foundations and piping connections that can accommodate movement, and a plan for inspecting tanks after a strong earthquake. When a tank is reconstructed or relocated, its design is checked against API 650, which carries seismic design rules in an annex. The current Body of Knowledge leaves that annex and the earthquake thickness calculations out of the exam, so this is knowledge for the job.

Winter adds two further questions. Fixed roofs carry snow, which is one of the loads API 650 designs roofs for, so a thinned roof deserves attention before the snow arrives rather than after. And cold metal raises the brittle fracture question that API 653 addresses in its own section on assessing that risk, particularly for older tanks whose plate toughness is unknown.

Worked example: a fixed roof after a snowy winter

API 653 requires roof plates corroded to an average thickness of less than 0.09 inch in any 100 square inches, or with any holes through the plate, to be repaired or replaced. This example uses illustrative figures. A cone-roof tank at a Salt Lake terminal was built 20 years ago with 3/16-inch roof plate, 0.1875 inch. An inspector takes nine ultrasonic readings in each of two 10-inch by 10-inch squares, measuring from a safe working position rather than walking a roof of unknown thickness.

  1. Area A, open roof: 0.112, 0.105, 0.098, 0.101, 0.094, 0.099, 0.108, 0.103 and 0.097 inch. The sum is 0.917, so the average is 0.917 ÷ 9 = 0.102 inch. That is above 0.09 inch, so the area is acceptable today.
  2. Area B, beside a vent where condensate collects: 0.092, 0.081, 0.077, 0.088, 0.070, 0.085, 0.094, 0.083 and 0.079 inch. The sum is 0.749, so the average is 0.083 inch. That is below 0.09 inch, so the plate in that area must be repaired or replaced.
  3. Looking ahead for Area A: it has lost 0.1875 − 0.102 = 0.0855 inch in 20 years, about 0.0043 inch a year. At that rate it reaches 0.09 inch in (0.102 − 0.09) ÷ 0.0043, which is about 2.8 years.

The practical answer is to replace the corroded plate in Area B now and plan the rest of the roof before the next external inspection, because Area A will fall below the limit well inside a five-year gap. On the exam the arithmetic is simple; what matters is knowing the 0.09-inch and 100-square-inch criterion well enough to apply it without hunting for the clause.

Routes into API 653 for Salt Lake tank people

API 653 eligibility follows Annex D of the standard: education plus experience within the last ten years, gained while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency. An engineering or technology degree needs one year in supervising or performing tank inspection; a two-year degree or certificate needs two years in tank design, fabrication, repair, operation or inspection, one of them in inspection; a high school diploma needs three years on the same terms; and no formal education needs five or more. The API 653 certification page covers the details. Locally, the usual entrants are terminal and tank-farm staff moving into inspection roles, tank construction and repair welders, and NDT technicians who run floor scans and shell thickness surveys. Atlantis's NDT training in Salt Lake City includes the ASNT SNT-TC-1A methods those technicians use, among them MFL.

Studying API 653 around terminal outages

API 653 work comes in bursts: a tank out of service for an internal inspection keeps a team busy for weeks, then the pace drops. A self-paced course fits that rhythm. Use the quiet periods for the open-book skills, chiefly moving between API 653 and API 650 in the PDFs and finding tables quickly, and use the busy periods to connect what you inspect with the clauses that govern it. Alongside API 653 and API 650, the current Body of Knowledge lists API RP 571, RP 575, RP 577, RP 652, selected sections of RP 651 and RP 576, and ASME Sections V and IX. The API 653 tank inspection guide is a useful companion before you start the full standard. Study the editions on the Publications Effectivity Sheet for your exam window, and send the instructor any question where the two standards seem to disagree.

Sponsoring tank inspectors from a Salt Lake refinery, terminal or plant

Refineries, pipeline and terminal operators, smelter and chemical storage owners and inspection contractors can enrol one candidate or several, and fees are quoted on request. A contractor covering tanks in Salt Lake, Cedar City and southern Idaho can prepare its inspectors without bringing them together, because each works through the material on their own schedule. API sets eligibility, administers the exam and issues the certification, and each candidate applies individually.

faq.q: Is there an API 653 course I can attend in person in Salt Lake City?
faq.a: Atlantis does not run one. Its API 653 course is online and self-paced, with an instructor answering questions, so you can prepare from Salt Lake City or from a terminal elsewhere. The exam itself must be taken in person at a Prometric test centre, and Prometric lists test centres in and around Salt Lake City that you can select when you schedule.

faq.q: Does Utah's aboveground petroleum storage tank programme require API 653 inspections?
faq.a: No. Utah's programme, run by the Division of Environmental Response and Remediation since 2021, covers certain petroleum tanks over 500 gallons and relies on registration, financial responsibility and tightness testing. It excludes petroleum refiners and bulk stations and terminals altogether, so the large refinery and terminal tanks in the valley are inspected under federal rules and owners' own programmes instead.

faq.q: Our terminal tanks fall under SPCC. Does the rule require API 653 specifically?
faq.a: Not by name. The SPCC rule requires each aboveground bulk storage container to be tested or inspected for integrity on a regular schedule and after material repairs, using industry standards the owner selects and records in the plan. EPA names API 653 and STI SP001 as two commonly used standards. For field-erected steel tanks built to API 650, API 653 is the usual choice.

faq.q: Can a pipeline breakout tank in Utah use API 653's risk-based internal inspection interval?
faq.a: Not under the current federal rule. 49 CFR 195.432 requires breakout tanks to be inspected according to API 653 but excludes section 6.4.3, the risk-based internal interval. PHMSA proposed in June 2026 to allow risk-based intervals with upper limits; until a final rule is published, the exclusion stands. Refinery tanks that are not breakout tanks are not affected.

faq.q: Do heated waxy crude tanks change what I need to study for the exam?
faq.a: Not much for the exam, which tests API 653, the examined parts of API 650 and the listed recommended practices for any tank. They change a great deal at work: insulation, heating coils, wax on the floor and elevated temperatures all affect how you inspect. Learn the damage mechanisms heat accelerates, and how API 653 evaluates a tank in service.

faq.q: Is seismic design on the API 653 exam?
faq.a: No, on the current Body of Knowledge, which excludes API 650's seismic annex and the thickness calculations for wind, earthquake and small internal pressures. Check the Body of Knowledge for your own window. At work in Salt Lake City seismic design matters when a tank is reconstructed, relocated or re-rated, and after any strong earthquake, when anchorage and the shell-to-bottom junction need inspecting.

faq.q: I run MFL floor scans for a contractor. Does that count as API 653 experience?
faq.a: Floor scanning is tank inspection work, so it can count if your employer was an authorized inspection agency, or you worked under contract to one, and API can verify your role. With a high school diploma you need three years in tank work, including one in supervising or performing inspection; a two-year technical qualification reduces that to two years.

faq.q: Can a terminal operator enrol inspectors working at several sites?
faq.a: Yes. Operators and contractors with staff in Salt Lake, southern Utah, Idaho or Nevada can enrol a group, and fees are quoted on request. Each inspector studies on their own schedule and asks the instructor their own questions, which suits teams that are rarely in the same place. Each candidate applies to API and meets its eligibility rules individually.
